section.title: Against False Prophets
section.sectionRationale: Jerusalem's true danger was never only the Babylonian army; it was the prophets and prophetesses who papered over that danger with comforting lies. Ezekiel exposes both the male prophets who whitewash a crumbling wall with false peace and the women who traffic in magic charms, warning that leaders who tell people what they want to hear will fall with the very structures they falsely reinforced.
section.thesis: God condemns prophets who speak from their own imagination rather than His true word, promising peace where there is no peace and propping up a doomed city with whitewash instead of truth, showing that false comfort is more dangerous than open warning, and that only the true Word of God, ultimately Christ Himself, can be trusted to build on solid ground.
section.frameNote: Three movements: woe pronounced on prophets who follow their own spirit and have seen nothing true; the image of a flimsy wall whitewashed with false peace, doomed to fall in the coming storm; and woe pronounced on prophetesses who ensnare souls with magic charms for a handful of barley.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who are now prophesying. Tell those who prophesy out of their own imagination: Hear the word of the LORD!
This is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit, yet have seen nothing.
Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes among the ruins.
You did not go up to the gaps or restore the wall around the house of Israel so that it would stand in the battle on the Day of the LORD.
They see {{chazon_shav|false visions}} and speak lying divinations. They claim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ when the LORD did not send them; yet they wait for the fulfillment of their message.
Haven’t you seen a false vision and spoken a lying divination when you proclaim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ even though I have not spoken?
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD.

My hand will be against the prophets who see false visions and speak lying divinations. They will not belong to the council of My people or be recorded in the register of the house of Israel, nor will they enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.

units.label: The whitewashed wall
units.note: false peace over a crumbling foundation

verses.text: Because they have led My people astray, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace, and whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built,
tell those {{tapel|whitewashing}} the wall that it will fall. Rain will come in torrents, I will send hailstones plunging down, and a windstorm will burst forth.
Surely when the wall has fallen, you will not be asked, ‘Where is the whitewash with which you covered it?’
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: In My wrath I will release a windstorm, and in My anger torrents of rain and hail will fall with destructive fury.

I will tear down the wall you whitewashed and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is exposed. The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
And after I have vented My wrath against the wall and against those who whitewashed it, I will say to you: ‘The wall is gone, and so are those who whitewashed it,
those prophets of Israel who prophesied to Jerusalem and saw a vision of peace for her when there was no peace, declares the Lord GOD.’
Now, O son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy out of their own imagination. Prophesy against them

and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the women who sew {{kesatot|magic charms}} on their wrists and make veils for the heads of people of every height, in order to ensnare their souls. Will you ensnare the souls of My people but preserve your own?

You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. By lying to My people who would listen, you have killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived.

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: See, I am against the magic charms with which you ensnare souls like birds, and I will tear them from your arms. So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds.
I will also tear off your veils and deliver My people from your hands, so that they will no longer be prey in your hands. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
Because you have disheartened the righteous with your lies, even though I have caused them no grief, and because you have encouraged the wicked not to turn from their evil ways to save their lives,
therefore you will no longer see false visions or practice divination. I will deliver My people from your hands. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

chazon_shav.gloss: False, empty, or worthless vision. These prophets claimed genuine revelation, 'Thus declares the LORD,' while seeing nothing real, manufacturing comforting messages from their own imagination rather than receiving them from God.

tapel.gloss: Whitewash, or untempered plaster smeared over a weak wall to hide its cracks. The image pictures false prophets covering Jerusalem's real, structural danger with a thin, cosmetic layer of reassurance that cannot survive the coming storm.

kesatot.gloss: Magic bands or charms sewn onto the wrists, used in occult practices claiming to control or manipulate life and death. God tears these very charms from the prophetesses' arms, showing His power to free the souls their sorcery had ensnared.

basic.context: Jerusalem faced a danger even greater than the coming Babylonian siege: prophets and prophetesses who told the people exactly what they wanted to hear. Ezekiel exposes both groups, the men who whitewashed a crumbling wall with false assurances of peace, and the women who used magic charms to manipulate and profit from vulnerable souls.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a direct, historical indictment of specific religious leaders operating among Ezekiel's exiled community and in Jerusalem, not a general parable. The plain, uncomfortable truth is that comforting words are not automatically true words, and that God holds those who claim to speak for Him to the strictest account when they have not.
basic.originalLanguages: These prophets peddle a chazon shav, an empty or worthless vision, dressed up in the language of true revelation. Their message is tapel, whitewash, a thin cosmetic covering over real structural danger. The prophetesses use kesatot, magic charms, literally binding people's wrists with occult manipulation for a handful of barley.
basic.typology: The whitewashed wall that looks solid but cannot withstand the storm anticipates Jesus' parable of the wise and foolish builders, Matthew 7:24-27, where only a house built on the rock of His words stands when the storm comes; false comfort, however sincere, cannot substitute for a true foundation.
basic.christ: Jesus repeatedly warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15, and who will arise claiming great signs, Matthew 24:24, standing in direct continuity with Ezekiel's warning; and where these prophets falsely cried 'Peace, peace' when there was no peace, Christ alone is the one who can truly say 'Peace I leave with you', John 14:27, because His peace is secured by an atonement that actually deals with sin rather than papering over it.
basic.god: God is jealous for the truth of His own name; He will not let those who falsely claim to speak for Him escape accountability, and He is personally committed to freeing the souls ensnared by manipulative religion, tearing the very charms from the deceivers' arms.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 6:14 records the same charge, 'They have healed the brokenness of My people superficially, saying, Peace, peace, but there is no peace.' Matthew 7:15-23 and 24:24 warn of false prophets and false christs. Matthew 7:24-27 contrasts building on rock versus sand. 1 John 4:1 commands testing every spirit.
basic.oneStory: This is the exposure of religious deception at its most dangerous, comforting words mistaken for God's true word. Jesus stands in continuity with this warning, cautioning His own followers against false prophets, and offers Himself as the only sure foundation and the only true peace, one that can actually withstand the storm these whitewashed walls could not.

context.literary:
Ezekiel 13 is a single oracle in two panels, and each panel is built from the same three beats: a command to prophesy against a group, a woe that exposes what the group does, and a closing promise that God will act so that 'you will know that I am the LORD.' That recognition formula falls in verse 9, verse 14, verse 21 and verse 23, so the chapter is stitched together by the one outcome God is after. The first panel, verses 1 to 16, is addressed to the prophets and carries two images, the foxes among ruins and the whitewashed wall. The second, verses 17 to 23, turns to the women and trades walls for wrists, veils and snares.

The images are chosen to answer each other. Foxes, or jackals, make their homes in rubble and do nothing to rebuild it; they live off the city's collapse. A wall exists to be repaired, and verse 5 names the work the prophets skipped, going up to the gaps. Instead of mending, they plaster. The chapter then lets weather do what the prophets would not do, so the plaster and the flimsy wall are tested by the same storm in verses 11 to 14.

Notice the verbs of seeing. The false prophets 'see' (the verb of visions) and yet 'have seen nothing,' verse 3. Their claim to vision is empty, and their claim to speak for God is theft of a formula, 'Thus declares the LORD,' verse 6. The chapter sits between the dated vision cycle of chapters 8 to 11, where the glory leaves the temple, and the chapters on elders, the vine and the bride that follow. Together they explain why the exiles still believe Jerusalem is safe: they have been told so, and Ezekiel 12:24 has already promised an end to flattering divinations. Chapter 13 delivers that end.
context.historical:
Ezekiel is in Babylonia among the exiles deported with Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and Jerusalem still stands. The comfortable message he is attacking was in circulation on both ends of the road. In Jerusalem, Jeremiah met the prophet Hananiah, who promised that the yoke of Babylon would be broken within two years and the temple vessels returned, Jeremiah 28:2-4. In Babylon, Jeremiah wrote to the exiles that they should not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among them, Jeremiah 29:8-9, and he named two men, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar would put to death, Jeremiah 29:21. Ezekiel's oracle is the third voice in the same debate, and it shows the exiles were not a separate world but a mirror of Jerusalem.

The whitewash is a building detail every hearer knew. A wall of loose stone or mud brick was coated with lime plaster to give it a finished face. A wet season finds the weakness underneath, and a storm of rain, hail and wind in verses 11 to 14 is precisely what such a wall cannot take. The wall is also a political image. Jerusalem's defense depended on its fortifications, and the prophets were telling the court that diplomacy and city walls would hold against Babylon.

The prophetesses are the other surprise. Israel had real women prophets, among them Miriam, Deborah and Huldah, and the postexilic period still knew a Noadiah, who tried to intimidate Nehemiah, Nehemiah 6:14. The charge here is therefore not that women prophesy but that these women, like the men, 'prophesy out of their own imagination,' verse 17, and that they trade their services for 'handfuls of barley and scraps of bread,' verse 19. The practice is a paid folk-religion of charms and veils, aimed at life and death decisions: who will die and who will live.
context.canonical:
Ezekiel 13 is one of the clearest testimonies in the Prophets to a problem the Torah had already anticipated. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 and 18:20 define the false prophet by two tests, the one who leads to other gods and the one who speaks in the LORD's name what He has not commanded, and Deuteronomy 18:20 sets the penalty of death. Ezekiel is carrying out that law by prophetic word rather than by courtroom. His verse 9 is its sentence: no place in the council, no entry in the register, no return to the land.

The same charge runs through the prophetic books. Jeremiah 6:14 describes the 'Peace, peace' dressing of a wound, and Jeremiah 23:16 says such prophets 'speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.' Micah 3:5 condemns prophets who 'proclaim peace' for those who feed them, and Isaiah 30:10 records the people's own demand, 'Speak to us pleasant words.' Lamentations 2:14 looks back after the fall and names what Ezekiel has said beforehand: the visions were empty and deceptive and did not expose Jerusalem's guilt. Ezekiel 22:28 returns to the whitewash image almost word for word.

The New Testament inherits the pattern. Jesus warns of false prophets, Matthew 7:15 and 24:24, and then ends the Sermon on the Mount with a house that stands or falls in a storm, Matthew 7:24-27. Paul warns that people will gather teachers who suit their own desires, 2 Timothy 4:3-4, and Acts 20:29-30 predicts distortion arising from within the flock. John gives the test in one sentence, 'test the spirits to see whether they are from God,' 1 John 4:1. The canonical line is steady: God does not leave His people without a means of telling a true word from a counterfeit.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to stop treating a pleasant message as evidence that it came from God. His first hearers were people who badly wanted to go home and who had prophets telling them they soon would. The chapter breaks that link between what comforts and what is true. The test it offers is source and result, not mood. Did the LORD send them, verse 6? Did they go up to the gaps and do the hard work of repair, verse 5? Did their word turn the wicked back from their ways, verse 22? A prophet who passes none of these is false however warm the room feels.

He also wanted them to see that false comfort is a kind of cruelty. The prophets 'disheartened the righteous with your lies' and encouraged 'the wicked not to turn from their evil ways to save their lives,' verse 22. Lies hurt in both directions, wounding those who are doing right and releasing those who are doing wrong. The women 'killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived,' verse 19, so the stakes were life and death, not taste.

Finally, Ezekiel meant to give the faithful hope. God says, 'I will free the souls you have ensnared' and 'I will deliver My people from your hands,' verses 20 to 23. The same chapter that condemns the deceivers promises that their spell will be broken. The audience is meant to hear both the warning and the rescue.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records God's judgment on particular prophets and prophetesses of the sixth century BC. Nothing in it commands a reader to track down modern deceivers or to treat every comforting preacher with suspicion. What carries forward is the principle that every claim to speak for God stands under His word, and that church leaders, writers and teachers of every age are answerable for it.

The practices named here, wrist charms and head veils for a handful of barley, are not prescribed for anyone; they describe what was condemned. Care is needed with the sentence in verse 9, which excludes the false prophets from the community. That describes what God Himself will do in Ezekiel's day, not a warrant for believers to cast out fellow believers whose teaching they dislike. Disagreement about secondary matters is not the sin here, and the New Testament separates it from deliberate distortion of the gospel, Galatians 1:8-9.

The applicable lessons are for the speaker and the hearer alike. A teacher is to say what God has said and to repair what is broken instead of covering it. A hearer is to ask not only whether a message encourages but whether it is true, Acts 17:11, remembering Jesus' own sobering line in Luke 6:26, 'Woe to you when all men speak well of you.'

debates.question: How can God say the false prophets 'wait for the fulfillment' of what He never spoke?

views.label: They expected to be vindicated by events
views.case: Verse 6 says they 'wait for the fulfillment of their message.' On this reading, the prophets sincerely or cynically expected events to bear them out, and the chapter shows how the pressure of an unfolding crisis sometimes drives self-deceived people to keep predicting. The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC then served as the test Deuteronomy 18:22 describes, in which a word that does not come to pass was never from the LORD.

views.label: They hoped to confirm the word by their own efforts
views.case: The Hebrew idea is of making a word stand or come true. Some take this to mean the prophets were working to bring about what they had said, using the very charms and rites of the women in verses 18 to 20, or leaning on political schemes, instead of waiting on God.

debates.bearing: Either way the point is the same: the fulfillment they awaited would not come, because God had not spoken. Their confidence is no evidence of their call, and the chapter teaches readers to judge by whether God sent the word, not by how sure the speaker is.

debates.question: What were the 'magic charms' and 'veils' of verse 18?

views.label: Instruments of sympathetic magic or divination
views.case: The most common reading takes them as ritual items worn or made to bind or release a person's life force, used in rites of binding that claimed to decide who would live and who would die. This fits the language of ensnaring souls like birds, verse 20, and the charge in verse 19 about killing and sparing.

views.label: A practice we cannot reconstruct
views.case: The Hebrew nouns are obscure, and what the women actually did is not described anywhere else in Scripture. A cautious reading says only what the text says: these were instruments of manipulation, sold for a pittance, which pretended to hold power over life and death.

debates.bearing: The precise rite does not change the verdict, because God's charge is about what it does to people (it ensnares souls, profanes His name and misleads the righteous and the wicked) rather than about how the instruments were made.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the preposition in verse 2. The prophets prophesy 'out of their own imagination,' which in Hebrew is simply 'from their own heart,' the same expression Jeremiah 23:16 puts as 'from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.' The contrast is between two sources, heart and mouth. Verse 3 sharpens it: they 'follow their own spirit,' literally they walk after their own ruach. The word is the same one used of the divine Spirit who enters Ezekiel, so the chapter sets a human spirit that leads a prophet against the Spirit of the LORD who sends him.

The pair 'false visions' and 'lying divinations' in verses 6 to 9 uses a related set of terms: shav, emptiness or worthlessness, and kazav, a lie. Shav is the word of the third commandment, 'take the name of the LORD in vain,' Exodus 20:7, and the reach is wide. To say 'Thus declares the LORD' when the LORD has not sent you is to take His name for a vain purpose. Verse 7 is a rhetorical question with a grammatical force: 'Haven't you seen a false vision?' calls the prophets to admit what they know.

The image of verse 5 is exact. The 'gaps' are breaches in a wall, and to 'go up to the gaps' is to climb into a breach in battle. In Ezekiel 22:30 the same field of imagery returns when God says He searched for a man 'to repair the wall and stand in the gap' and found no one. The prophets' failure is not only that they lied but that they would not stand where the wall was broken.

The key word of verses 10 to 15 is tapel, 'whitewash,' with the sense of something flimsy or insipid, and the same word turns up in Ezekiel 22:28 and in the pair 'empty and deceptive' of Lamentations 2:14. The verb behind 'whitewashing' means to smear over. Note also that God does not say the wall will be mended better, but that the storm will 'tear down' the wall until 'its foundation is exposed,' verse 14. The plaster was a cover for a missing foundation, and the foundation is what the storm reveals.

In verse 9 the false prophets are excluded from the 'council' of My people. The Hebrew sod is the circle of confidants, and Jeremiah 23:18 and 23:22 use it for the heavenly council where a true prophet stands and hears the word. To be shut out of the sod is to be shown never to have stood there. Alongside it comes the 'register' or written record of the house of Israel, which points to a roll of the restored community. The word 'souls' in verses 18 to 20 is nephesh, a person's life, which is why the prophetesses' ensnaring is a matter of life and death, not of mere persuasion.

typology.type: The wall that falls in the storm, Ezekiel 13:10-16
typology.fulfillment: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders, one on rock and one on sand, and the same storm of rain, torrents and wind strikes both, Matthew 7:24-27. The difference is not the weather but the foundation, and Jesus defines the foundation as hearing His words and acting on them. Paul says that 'no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:11. The type falls short because Ezekiel's wall is already condemned, whereas Jesus offers a foundation that holds; His house stands because of the rock, not because of repairs.

typology.type: The prophets who fed themselves, Ezekiel 13:19
typology.fulfillment: The women trade their word for barley and bread. The pattern of the false teacher who serves his own appetite recurs in Philippians 3:19 and Romans 16:18, and Peter says that 'in their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words,' 2 Peter 2:3. The true prophet answers the opposite way: Jesus gave Himself rather than feeding on His flock, John 10:11. The type is a warning more than a promise, and it finds its remedy in the Shepherd who lays down His life.

typology.type: Peace pronounced over a threatened city, Ezekiel 13:10
typology.fulfillment: The cry of 'Peace' while destruction waits finds an echo in Paul's warning about the Day of the Lord, 'While people are saying, "Peace and security," destruction will come upon them suddenly,' 1 Thessalonians 5:3. In Christ the peace that false prophets only claimed is actually made, for 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and He has torn down the wall of hostility between God and sinners and between people. The correspondence is of contrast: Ezekiel's wall of false peace falls, and Christ tears down a wall of real hostility.

study.christ:
Ezekiel 13 leads to Christ by contrast first. Where the prophets say 'Peace' with nothing behind it, Jesus gives what the false prophets could only claim: 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' John 14:27. The difference is the ground. His peace is founded on a death that deals with the thing that makes peace impossible. Paul says of Him, 'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. A prophet who whitewashes sin offers peace without a cross; Jesus offers peace by one.

It leads to Christ by pattern. The chapter's false prophets never stood in the gap, verse 5, and in Ezekiel 22:30 God says He searched for someone to stand in it and found no one. The New Testament portrays Christ as the answer to that search. Isaiah 59:16 says God saw there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation, and Hebrews 7:25 says Jesus 'always lives to intercede.' The man who goes up to the breach is the Son who goes to the cross.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the true Prophet. Deuteronomy 18:15 promised a prophet like Moses, and Jesus is that prophet because He speaks only what the Father gives Him, John 12:49-50. The false prophets 'follow their own spirit,' but Jesus says, 'The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life,' John 6:63. When He says that a house is built on the rock of 'these words of Mine,' Matthew 7:24, He is claiming for His own speech the authority that the false prophets only counterfeited.

It leads to Christ through the rescue promised to the ensnared. God says, 'I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds,' verse 20. Psalm 124:7 uses the same picture for a rescued person, 'We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler.' In the gospel, Jesus announces freedom to captives, Luke 4:18, and Hebrews 2:15 says He frees those who were held in slavery by fear of death. The false prophetesses held people with fear; the Messiah breaks fear's hold.

One guard against forcing the text: Ezekiel 13 does not say that the wall or the veils are pictures of Christ. The links come from the Gospels' own handling of false prophecy, rock and storm, and from the broader pattern of a faithful Shepherd contrasted with faithless ones, Ezekiel 34. What the chapter supplies is the problem and the demand, and Christ is the person who answers both.
study.god:
The chapter shows first a God who cares about the integrity of His own speech. He is not content to be misquoted. Three times He says 'I am against you' or 'My hand will be against,' verses 8, 9 and 20, and the offense He names is that men and women have put words in His mouth: 'when the LORD did not send them,' verse 6, 'even though I have not spoken,' verse 7. The God of Israel speaks, and a counterfeit of His speech is therefore a kind of identity theft against Him and an assault on His people.

It shows a God who cares more for His people than for their comfort. A pleasant lie would have been the easier thing for Him to tolerate, and in some seasons He lets people have what they ask for, Isaiah 30:10. But here He sends the storm so that the wall's real condition is exposed. Love that leaves a person comforted in a falling building is not love. His wrath in verses 13 and 14 is the severity of One who refuses to let His people shelter in a lie.

It shows a God who protects the vulnerable from those who profit from them. The prophetesses prey on the ordinary person who pays for a charm, and God says He will 'deliver My people from your hands, so that they will no longer be prey in your hands,' verse 21. The same God who pronounces judgment declares Himself the defender of those caught in manipulative religion, in a way that anticipates the Shepherd who seeks the scattered in Ezekiel 34.

It shows God as the one who knows the heart and the source. Verse 22 says He had caused the righteous 'no grief,' and it is the prophets' lies that grieved them. God's care for the righteous is personal; their sorrow offends Him. It shows His desire for the wicked too, for verse 22 charges the prophets with encouraging evildoers 'not to turn from their evil ways to save their lives.' The Lord's deepest wish is that the wicked turn and live, as Ezekiel 18:23 says; false peace stands in the way of that wish.

The tension the chapter holds is between severity and rescue. The same God who tears down the wall rescues the ensnared, and He sets limits on the damage: the prophets will 'no longer see false visions,' verse 23. For worship, the passage teaches reverence for His word. We are to receive what He has said, to be wary of any message that adds to it or removes its edge, and to trust that His truth, even when it is hard, is given as an act of care.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah's version of the charge in verse 10. The prophets dress a serious wound with very little care and say 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace at all. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, one in Jerusalem and one in exile, name the same sickness, which shows how widespread the pleasant lie had become.

Jeremiah's longest treatment of false prophets. They speak visions from their own minds, run without being sent, and have not stood in God's council. If they had stood there they would have turned the people from their evil ways. It supplies the test Ezekiel assumes: a true word calls for repentance.

The prophet Hananiah promises that within two years the yoke of Babylon will be broken and the temple's vessels returned. This is a concrete case of the 'vision of peace' in Ezekiel 13:16, and Jeremiah's later reply shows how the matter was settled, by events and by God's word.

Jeremiah writes to the exiles themselves, telling them not to be deceived by the prophets and diviners in their midst, who prophesy falsely in God's name. It places Ezekiel's target among the very community he addressed.

Ezekiel returns to the same picture: Jerusalem's prophets whitewash deeds by false visions and lying divinations, saying 'This is what the Lord GOD says' when the LORD has not spoken. Together with 22:30, where God finds no one to stand in the gap, it completes the portrait begun in chapter 13.

The Torah's test of a prophet. One who speaks in God's name what He has not commanded must die, and a word that does not come to pass was never His. Ezekiel's pronouncement in verse 9 is this law carried out through prophecy.

Written after the fall, it admits the point of Ezekiel 13: the visions of Jerusalem's prophets were empty and deceptive, and they did not expose the city's guilt to ward off captivity. It shows what the whitewash cost.

Jesus warns against false prophets and then closes the Sermon on the Mount with rock and sand, rain, torrents and wind. The storm tests the foundation, as in Ezekiel 13:11-14, and the foundation is obeying His words.

Paul foresees a time when people will not tolerate sound doctrine and will gather teachers to suit their own desires. It is the demand side of Ezekiel 13, the audience that wants pleasant words and so produces the prophets who supply them.

The apostle's command to test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out. It supplies the Christian counterpart of the question Ezekiel asks: did God send this word, and does it agree with what He has said?

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is a story of speech. God speaks the world into being in Genesis 1, and the first fracture comes when the serpent contests what God has said, Genesis 3:1. Ezekiel 13 is a late scene in that long conflict. The conflict is not between belief and unbelief but between two voices that both claim to be God's, and the book of Deuteronomy had already given Israel the means to tell them apart. What the chapter adds is the cost of failure: a city that trusts the wrong voice will stand behind plaster until the storm comes.

Looking back, the chapter explains why Jerusalem fell. The exiles will later admit it was not that God had failed to warn them but that their prophets had told them the warning was false. Lamentations 2:14 puts it in a line, and Ezekiel 12:24 and 13:23 promise the end of false visions. Looking forward, the chapter prepares for a renewal of speech itself. In Ezekiel 36:26-27 God promises a new heart and His own Spirit, so that His people will carry out His statutes. The remedy for the false spirit of the prophets, verse 3, is the gift of the true Spirit.

The story reaches its center in Jesus, the Word who was with God, John 1:1, who is faithful and true in every utterance. Where Israel's prophets whitewashed a wall, He becomes the foundation; where they cried 'Peace' without cause, He makes peace by His blood, Colossians 1:20. The New Testament then continues the warning for the church, in Matthew 24:24, 2 Peter 2:1 and 1 John 4:1, because the age between His comings is still an age of competing voices.

The story ends with the removal of the lie. In the new Jerusalem there is no counterfeit; Revelation 21:27 says nothing false will enter it, and 22:3-5 says the servants will see His face. The city that falls in Ezekiel 13 is replaced by one whose walls are named 'Salvation,' Isaiah 60:18, and whose foundations carry the names of the Lamb's twelve apostles, Revelation 21:14. Every wall plastered by a lie is finally answered by a city built on truth.

sermon.title: Genuine or False Prophets? (Ezek. 13-14)
sermon.why: Carson works directly through Ezekiel 13, contrasting false prophets who manufacture comforting visions from their own imagination with the marks of genuine, Spirit-given prophecy, drawing out principles for discernment that this study applies to the whitewashed wall and the magic charms alike.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental charge God brings against the prophets in verses 1-9?

options.text: They prophesy out of their own imagination, claiming 'Thus declares the LORD' when He never spoke to them.
options.note: Verses 2-3 and 6-7 make this charge explicit and repeated.

options.text: They refused to speak to the people at all.
options.note: The problem is that they spoke constantly, but falsely, not that they were silent.

options.text: They demanded too much payment for their services.
options.note: Payment is addressed later regarding the prophetesses, verse 19, but this initial charge concerns false, self-generated visions.

options.text: They correctly predicted judgment but were ignored.
options.note: The problem is the opposite: they predicted false peace and comfort, not accurate judgment.

quiz.q: What does the image of the whitewashed wall represent?

options.text: False prophets covering Jerusalem's real, structural danger with a thin layer of comforting reassurance that cannot survive God's coming judgment.
options.note: Verses 10-15 develop this image as a direct picture of false, superficial peace.

options.text: A genuine, well-built defense that successfully protected the city.
options.note: The wall is explicitly flimsy and doomed to fall, not a genuine defense.

options.text: The temple's literal architecture needing repair.
options.note: The wall is a metaphor for false assurance, not a literal architectural report.

options.text: A minor cosmetic issue with no real consequence.
options.note: The consequence is severe: the wall's collapse pictures the city's coming destruction.

quiz.q: What specific practice are the prophetesses in verses 17-23 condemned for?

options.text: Sewing magic charms on wrists and making veils to ensnare souls for profit, handfuls of barley and scraps of bread.
options.note: Verses 18-19 describe this exact practice and its motive of profit.

options.text: Refusing to prophesy at all out of fear.
options.note: They actively prophesied and practiced occult manipulation, rather than remaining silent.

options.text: Teaching the law faithfully but too strictly.
options.note: Their offense is manipulative sorcery for profit, not strict but faithful teaching.

options.text: Publicly opposing the male false prophets.
options.note: The text presents them as engaging in a parallel abuse, not as opponents of the male prophets.

quiz.q: What does God promise to do about the charms these women use?

options.text: Tear them from their arms and free the souls ensnared by them.
options.note: Verse 20 states God will personally tear away the charms and liberate the ensnared souls.

options.text: Bless the charms so they work for good instead.
options.note: God opposes and destroys the charms entirely; He does not repurpose them.

options.text: Ignore the charms since they have no real spiritual power.
options.note: God takes direct, personal action against them rather than ignoring the practice.

options.text: Allow the women to keep using them if they repent.
options.note: God's stated response is to tear the charms away and end the practice entirely, not to negotiate continued use.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate outcome God promises for these false prophets and prophetesses?

options.text: They will be excluded from the council of God's people, and their false visions and divinations will end.
options.note: Verses 9 and 23 both state this outcome, that their prophetic deception will be brought to an end and they will lose their standing among God's people.

options.text: They will be promoted to positions of greater national influence.
options.note: The passage promises their downfall and exclusion, the opposite of promotion.

options.text: They will be given a final chance to prophesy accurately.
options.note: The text describes ending their practice and influence, not granting further prophetic opportunity.

options.text: They will be forgiven immediately without consequence.
options.note: The passage describes real, severe consequences: exclusion from the community and the end of their false practices.

questions: The false prophets told people what they wanted to hear rather than what was true. Where in your own life do you prefer comforting words over honest ones, even at the cost of the truth?
The whitewashed wall looked solid but could not survive the storm. What false assurances or shortcuts are you relying on that might not hold up under real pressure or trial?
The prophetesses profited from ensnaring vulnerable souls with manipulative promises. Where might you be tempted to use spiritual language to control or manipulate others, even with good intentions?

God personally promises to tear the charms from the deceivers' arms and free the ensnared souls. Where do you need to trust that God actively fights for those trapped by false teaching or manipulation, rather than leaving them to escape alone?
Jesus warns that false prophets will come in sheep's clothing. What practical habits help you test what you hear, in preaching, online, or from trusted voices, against the actual word of God?

translationNotes.note: The comparison of the prophets to 'foxes among the ruins' pictures scavengers exploiting a broken-down city for their own advantage rather than repairing it, an image of self-interested leadership abandoning real responsibility.
This text reads verses 15 and 16 as a continuous sentence, identifying 'those who whitewashed it' directly with 'those prophets of Israel' in the following verse.

The exact nature of the 'magic charms' and 'veils' is debated among scholars, but the underlying Hebrew terms consistently point to items used in occult practices claiming power over life and death, exploited here for material profit.
